content: The contraceptive patch is a transdermal patch applied to the skin that releases synthetic estrogen and progestin hormones to prevent pregnancy. It is considered to have similar effectiveness to the combined oral contraceptive pill. Currently, the only available contraceptive patches are Ortho Evra, marketed in the United States by Ortho-McNeil, and Evra, marketed in Canada by Janssen-Ortho and in the United Kingdom and other countries by Janssen-Cilag. These patches are packaged in boxes of three and are available only by prescription. Informally, the contraceptive patch is often referred to as the Patch. Method of Use A woman applies her first patch to her upper outer arm, buttocks, abdomen, or thigh on either the first day of her menstrual cycle (Day 1) or the first Sunday following that day, depending on her preference. The day of application is then referred to as patch change day. Seven days later, on the next patch change day, the woman removes the patch and applies a new one to one of the approved locations on her body. This process is repeated weekly for three weeks. On the fourth patch change day, the patch is removed and not replaced, allowing for a seven-day patch-free interval. After this interval, a new patch is applied on the next patch change day. Backup Contraception If a woman begins using the patch on Day 1 of her menstrual cycle, the patch takes effect in time to prevent ovulation, and no backup contraception is needed. If the patch is started immediately after a first-trimester abortion or miscarriage, it is considered equivalent to a Day 1 start, and no backup contraception is required. However, if a woman begins using the patch on the first Sunday following Day 1 of her cycle, she must use a backup form of contraception, such as condoms or spermicide, for the first week of patch use. Mechanism of Action The contraceptive patch works primarily by preventing ovulation, similar to other combined hormonal contraceptives. A secondary mechanism involves altering cervical mucus to inhibit sperm penetration. Hormonal contraceptives may also have effects on the endometrium that could theoretically affect implantation, although no scientific evidence supports that prevention of implantation occurs with their use. The Ortho Evra patch contains 750 µg of ethinyl estradiol (an estrogen) and 6000 µg of norelgestromin (a progestin), while the Evra patch contains 600 µg of ethinyl estradiol and 6000 µg of norelgestromin. Both patches are designed to release approximately 20 µg/day of ethinyl estradiol and 150 µg/day of norelgestromin into the systemic circulation. Interactions and Contraindications The effectiveness of the contraceptive patch, like other hormonal contraceptives, may be significantly reduced when co-administered with certain antibiotics, antifungals, anticonvulsants, or other drugs that increase the metabolism of contraceptive steroids. However, a clinical pharmacokinetic study showed that oral administration of tetracycline HCl 500 mg for three days prior to and seven days during the use of Ortho Evra did not reduce its effectiveness. This finding is important, as tetracycline-derived antibiotics are often prescribed following an abortion to prevent infection when synthetic hormone contraceptives are to be used afterward. Drugs containing St. John’s Wort are also known to affect the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Side Effects In three large clinical trials involving 3,330 women using the Ortho Evra/Evra patch for up to one year, 12% of users discontinued the patch due to adverse events. The most frequently reported adverse events included breast discomfort, engorgement, or pain (22%), headache (21%), application site reactions (17%), nausea (17%), upper respiratory tract infections (10%), menstrual cramps (10%), and abdominal pain (9%). Breakthrough bleeding and/or spotting were reported by 18% of users in cycle 1, 12% in cycle 3, 8% in cycle 6, and cycle 13. Breakthrough bleeding requiring more than one pad or tampon per day was reported by 4% in cycle 1, 3% in cycles 3 and 6, and 1% in cycle 13. Additional side effect information is available in the Ortho Evra label information and the Evra SPC and PIL. Thromboembolic Risks All combined hormonal contraceptives carry a small increased risk of serious or fatal thromboembolic events. Research is ongoing to compare the thromboembolic risks of Ortho Evra to those of combined oral contraceptive pills. One study found that users of the contraceptive patch may have a twofold increased risk of non-fatal venous thromboembolic events compared to women taking a norgestimate-containing oral contraceptive with 35 µg of estrogen. However, another study concluded that the risk of non-fatal venous thromboembolism for the patch is similar to that of oral contraceptives containing 35 µg of ethinyl estradiol and norgestimate. The contradictory findings between these studies are unresolved due to overlapping confidence intervals. In 2004, the Associated Press reported that fatal adverse events were reported to the FDA for Ortho Evra users at three times the rate of fatal events in oral contraceptive users. However, these comparisons are not based on methodical scientific studies. The Ortho Evra package insert advises women using hormonal contraceptives, including Ortho Evra, not to smoke, as the risk of cardiovascular disease (such as thromboembolism) is significantly increased in women over 35 who smoke. The manufacturer notes that the patch introduces 60% higher levels of estrogen into the bloodstream compared to oral contraceptives, though the clinical significance of this difference is unknown. In November 2005, Ortho McNeil, in conjunction with the FDA, revised the Ortho Evra label to include a bolded warning about higher estrogen exposure and the potential increased risk of blood clots. Lawsuits The contraceptive patch has been associated with strokes and thrombosis, and its mechanism of hormone absorption and dissipation differs from that of oral contraceptives. Several lawsuits have been filed over these issues. For example, a lawsuit filed in federal court in New Jersey in September 2005 by a Georgia woman who suffered a pulmonary embolism alleged that the company promoted the patch despite knowledge of its health risks for financial gain while failing to warn of the risks of blood clots and other injuries. In November 2005, CBS News reported on documents from a lawsuit involving a young mother who was paralyzed by a stroke, revealing that the company had received nearly 500 reports of adverse events between April 2002 and December 2004. During the same period, only 61 adverse event reports were filed for all types of birth control pills. The parents of a 14-year-old girl from Wisconsin also filed a lawsuit against Johnson & Johnson, claiming that she died from a blood clot caused by her use of the patch.
